subsection: 6. War and revolution in Germany, and the Peace Settlement, 1918–1920

notes.h: Collapse of the Central Powers and revolution in Germany
notes.b: By autumn 1918 the German army could not win, and the collapse of the home front led to revolution and the end of the monarchy.
points: Ludendorff asked for an armistice in late September 1918, and Prince Max of Baden became Chancellor on 3 October 1918 to negotiate it.
Sailors at Kiel mutinied at the end of October 1918, refusing orders for a final naval attack, and the mutiny spread to other ports and cities.
Workers' and soldiers' councils took power in many German cities in early November 1918, on the Russian model.
Wilhelm II abdicated on 9 November 1918, and the Social Democrat Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed a German republic in Berlin the same day.
The Social Democrat Friedrich Ebert became head of the provisional government, and he reached an agreement with the army leadership to suppress radicalism.
The Spartacist rising of January 1919 in Berlin was crushed by Freikorps units, and Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were murdered after their arrest.
The Weimar National Assembly met in February 1919 in Weimar, away from the unrest in Berlin, and it drafted the constitution of the Weimar Republic.
Austria-Hungary's empire broke apart in October and November 1918, as the Habsburg government lost control of its nationalities.
The Czechs and Slovaks, Poles, Croats and Slovenes, and other nationalities declared independence or union with neighbouring states.
The peace settlement with Austria was the Treaty of St Germain of September 1919, which recognised the new states and forbade union with Germany.
The Treaty of Trianon of June 1920 reduced Hungary to about a third of its former territory, with millions of Hungarians placed under foreign rule.
The treaties of Neuilly with Bulgaria, of November 1919, and of Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire, of August 1920, completed the settlement of the defeated states.

notes.h: Wilson's Fourteen Points and the path to Paris
points: Woodrow Wilson set out his Fourteen Points in a speech to Congress on 8 January 1918, as the basis for a peace without annexations or indemnities.
The Points called for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, reduction of armaments, and the adjustment of colonial claims with the interests of the population concerned.
Points 9 to 13 proposed boundaries for Italy, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Poland and the Balkans, mostly based on national groups.
Point 14 called for a general association of nations to guarantee the independence and territorial integrity of all states, which became the League of Nations.
The Allies accepted the Fourteen Points as the basis for an armistice, but Britain and France reserved their right to press for reparations and changes to the German colonies.

notes.b: The Paris Peace Conference opened in January 1919 and was dominated by the Big Four, whose aims often conflicted.
points: The Big Four were Woodrow Wilson of the USA, David Lloyd George of Britain, Georges Clemenceau of France and Vittorio Orlando of Italy.
Clemenceau wanted security against Germany, including a weakened Germany and a Rhineland separated from it, and he sought the largest reparations he could obtain.
Lloyd George wanted a settlement that would limit French power in Europe and protect the British Empire's trade and naval position.
Orlando's Italy was disappointed by its territorial gains, and he left the conference in April 1919 after failing to obtain the port of Fiume, which led to the phrase mutilated victory.
Japan sought recognition of the principle of racial equality, which was rejected by the other powers, and it gained the former German rights in Shandong.

notes.b: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919, the fifth anniversary of the Sarajevo assassination, in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
points: Article 231, the war-guilt clause, made Germany and its allies responsible for causing all the loss and damage of the war, and it was the basis for reparations.
Germany lost about 13 per cent of its European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine, which returned to France, and the Saar was placed under League administration for fifteen years.
Germany lost its colonies, which were placed under League mandates administered by the victorious powers.
The Polish Corridor gave Poland access to the Baltic Sea, and Danzig became a Free City under League supervision.
The Rhineland was demilitarised, and the German army was limited to 100,000 men, with no air force, no tanks and a navy of restricted size.
Germany was forbidden to unite with Austria, and it was required to pay reparations to be fixed by a commission, which in 1921 set the total at 132 billion gold marks.
The German government, formed after the Kaiser's abdication, signed the treaty under protest, and many Germans called it a Diktat.
Plebiscites were held in disputed areas, including Schleswig in 1920, where northern districts voted to join Denmark and southern districts remained German.
Upper Silesia was divided after a plebiscite in March 1921 and an armed rising, with the League settling the final frontier in 1922.
South Tyrol, which was largely German-speaking, was given to Italy, and Sudetenland, which had a German-speaking population, was included in Czechoslovakia.
Wilson's principle of self-determination was not applied to the German-speaking populations of Austria or to the Hungarian minorities left in neighbouring states.

notes.h: The League of Nations and the US Senate
points: The League of Nations was established on 10 January 1920 with headquarters at Geneva, and its members included the victorious powers and most neutral states.
The League was not joined by Germany until 1926, and it was excluded from the Soviet Union until 1934.
The US Senate rejected the Treaty of Versailles in November 1919 and again in March 1920, mainly because Republicans objected to the League covenant.
The USA made a separate peace with Germany in 1921, which meant that Wilson's League was never supported by the country whose president had proposed it.

notes.b: Woodrow Wilson was the American president who took the USA into the war and proposed the Fourteen Points and the League of Nations, but he could not secure American support for the treaty.
points: Woodrow Wilson was born on 28 December 1856 in Staunton, Virginia, and was an academic who became president of Princeton University in 1902.
He was Governor of New Jersey from 1911 to 1913 and was elected President of the USA in 1912, serving until 1921.
He kept the USA neutral in 1914 and was re-elected in 1916 with the slogan that he had kept the country out of war.
He asked Congress to declare war on Germany on 2 April 1917, saying the world must be made safe for democracy, and Congress declared war on 6 April.
He proposed the Fourteen Points and the League of Nations, and he insisted on the League's inclusion in the treaty, even when Clemenceau and Lloyd George wanted a harsher settlement.

Contemporaries in Europe hailed him as a champion of peace, and crowds in Paris and other cities greeted him warmly; his opponents in the US Senate, led by Henry Cabot Lodge, distrusted his internationalism.

Historians disagree about his achievement: some praise him as the founder of a liberal internationalism, while others argue that his principles were applied selectively and that his refusal to compromise with the Senate cost the League its chance in the USA.
He suffered a stroke in October 1919, and his reputation and health declined during the final months of his presidency.

notes.b: The settlement is judged by whether it secured a lasting peace or sowed the seeds of future conflict.
points: Achievement: the settlement created new states based on national groups, including Poland and Czechoslovakia, and it established the League as a forum for international disputes.
Limit: the new states contained large minorities who were not satisfied, and the settlement left Germany, Hungary and Italy with grievances against the peace.
Achievement: the League of Nations settled several disputes in the 1920s, including the Aaland Islands question in 1921.
Limit: the USA stayed outside the League, and the League could not enforce its decisions without the great powers' support.
Contemporaries such as John Maynard Keynes, in The Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919), argued that reparations were excessive and would damage European recovery.

Later historians differ: some argue that the treaty was too harsh and encouraged German revisionism, while others argue that Germany's defeat and the peace terms were less severe than many Germans later claimed.

keyTerms.definition: The principle that peoples should be able to choose their own government and state, usually based on nationality, which was applied unevenly after 1918.
The clause in the Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, which made Germany and its allies responsible for the war and the basis for reparations.
Payments imposed on Germany to compensate the Allies for war damage, set by a commission at 132 billion gold marks in 1921.
The international organisation established in January 1920 to settle disputes between states and promote collective security.
Woodrow Wilson's January 1918 statement of war aims and peace principles, which formed the basis of the armistice.
The German term for a peace imposed without negotiation, used to describe the Treaty of Versailles.
